added_claim_errors: Says United credits 'usually run about a year from the original ticket date' and builds the draft around that. Unverifiable, and it ignores the DOT rule that a credit offered in lieu of a refund must stay valid at least 5 years.
Says the $412 is only 'very likely' refundable and that accepting a credit is 'generally' treated as choosing the alternative. The rule is unconditional, so the hedging understates the entitlement.
Draft asks for 'at least 12 months', which is below the 5-year minimum for a credit in lieu of a refund. The answer does not say so.
Relies on a KOMO news article as the 'summary of the rule' for the refund point. The 14 CFR part 260 link is checkable, but what the news summary says is unverified.

Quotes DOT as saying its policy 'applies irrespective of the reason for a cancellation' and cites 89 FR 32760 with a govinfo link. The citation looks plausible and matches the key's 'regardless of the reason', but I did not open it, so the exact wording is unverified.

Says a next-day-afternoon rebooking is 'also a significant change on its own'. This is redundant and loosely applied, since the refund right comes from the cancellation itself, and it is not in the key.

Says United Future Flight Credits 'can expire on a travel-by date tied to your original ticket date', citing united.com. Unverified, and it ignores the 5-year minimum for a credit in lieu of a refund.
Draft asks for 'at least 12 months from the date it is issued', which is below the 5-year minimum for a credit in lieu of a refund. The answer does not say so.

reasons: Both answers catch the false premise at the start and correctly say weather does not remove the cash-refund right. Both miss the 7-business-day deadline and the 5-year minimum for a credit in lieu of a refund. Both also draft the credit-acceptance message, which asks for only 12 months. B states the entitlement more firmly and quotes the final-rule language. It tells the person not to send the credit message if they want the money, and it supplies a ready sentence declining the rebooking and requesting a full $412 refund to the original payment method under 14 CFR part 260, which covers key point 5. A is shorter and says explicitly that accepting a credit ends the refund right, but it hedges ('very likely', 'generally', 'your call') and only offers to write the refund version later. A also asserts as fact that United credits 'usually run about a year' from the original ticket date. B's ready refund wording makes it the more actionable answer, though it is longer and still lets the person take the weaker option.
